query: Is catastrophic forgetting in neural networks actually erasing old information, or is something else going on geometrically in the feature space?

What is the manifold hypothesis in machine learning, and what would it mean for representation learning if high-dimensional data like images didn't actually lie near a smooth lower-dimensional manifold?

How do variational autoencoders and diffusion models differ in the way they transform a simple latent distribution into complex real-world data, given that both seem to be doing a similar kind of generative mapping?
Do large language models' self-reported personality traits actually predict how they behave in real tasks?
Why would intentionally including toxic content in an LLM's pre-training data actually make it easier to suppress toxic outputs later, rather than just making the model worse?
How effective is activation steering (inference-time intervention) compared to prompting or fine-tuning for reducing toxic language model outputs?

Why do large language models perform well on simple needle-in-a-haystack retrieval tests at long context lengths but fail badly on tasks that require reasoning over many parts of that same context, like finding all pairs of related items?
Under what conditions do multi-agent AI systems actually outperform a single agent, and when do they perform worse?
How does error amplification compare across centralized, decentralized, and independent multi-agent architectures?
What's the theoretical difference between using Q-functions versus advantage functions as process reward models for guiding multi-step reasoning, and why might advantage-based guidance be more sound?
Would building a more powerful AI monitor solve the problem of models hiding their true reasoning?
Does having a massive context window (like 1M tokens) actually help a model synthesize information better than a standard retrieval pipeline, or can it underperform?
Why don't improvements in retrieval quality metrics like NDCG or MAP reliably translate into better final answer quality in RAG pipelines?
Is there a mathematical explanation for why supervised fine-tuning tends to cause catastrophic forgetting compared to preference-based methods like DPO?
Why do vision-language mixture-of-experts models often fail at reasoning problems presented as images, even though they solve the identical problem correctly when it's given as plain text?
Why do large language models tend to go along with a patient's false medical assumption instead of correcting it the way a human doctor would?
Does adding retrieval-augmented generation actually make an AI system safer when answering medical questions that contain false assumptions?
How do different large language models compare in terms of accommodating dangerous medical misconceptions from patients?
How can a multi-agent LLM system update agent prompts and the connection graph when the optimization space is discrete and non-differentiable, ruling out standard backpropagation?
What role does Bayesian bandit routing with Thompson sampling play in dynamically selecting which agents collaborate on a given task in a multi-agent system?
How reliable is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) as a safety fix for medical AI systems, and are there cases where it actually makes outputs worse rather than better?

What are the tradeoffs between reasoning in continuous latent space versus generating explicit discrete reasoning tokens, in terms of efficiency, reliability, and whether the process counts as genuine reasoning rather than pattern completion?

When autonomous AI research agents report high success rates on scientific discovery tasks, how much should that number actually be trusted given known issues like biased candidate selection or reward hacking on proxy metrics?

What's the cost tradeoff of inference-time reasoning boosts—does doubling or multiplying the compute per query typically buy proportionally large accuracy gains, or is it a steep price for modest improvement?

Do the speed and cost gains that inference providers advertise from techniques like model quantization actually come without sacrificing reasoning accuracy, or is there an inherent accuracy tradeoff that provider marketing glosses over?
Does giving an LLM agent a persona tend to improve its performance on tasks, or can it actually degrade its reasoning and decision-making?
Is reinforcement learning post-training capable of unlocking genuinely new capabilities in a language model, or is it fundamentally bounded by what the base model already learned during pretraining?

Why does high pass@1 or benchmark accuracy on math/reasoning tasks often fail to reflect genuine step-by-step reasoning ability in large language models, and what mechanisms have been proposed to explain this gap?
When multiple AI agents collaborate as a team, does adding more agents actually improve performance and reliability, or does it tend to introduce new risks and errors instead?

In multi-agent AI systems, does explicitly telling the group which agent is the expert or trusted identity actually make the group's decisions better and safer, or can that kind of trust signal fail to help or even be exploited?

In multi-agent AI systems, is it more effective to detect and isolate compromised agents after an attack has started, or to make individual agents inherently more resistant to being manipulated in the first place?

Does giving a language model more chain-of-thought reasoning length or more inference-time compute reliably improve its accuracy, or can extra reasoning actually make performance worse depending on the task?
If chain-of-thought monitoring fails to catch misaligned model behavior, would building a more powerful monitor model actually fix the problem, or is the failure rooted somewhere else?

When automatically optimizing a multi-agent AI system, does most of the performance gain come from optimizing each agent's individual prompt or from optimizing how the agents are arranged (the topology)?

For LLM agents that need to take actions, is it better for them to call tools through JSON-formatted function calls or by writing and executing actual code, and what's the reasoning behind each approach?
Why do vision-language AI models often correctly perceive what's in an image but still fail to solve a reasoning problem that they answer correctly when the same problem is given as plain text?

When reasoning models like o1 or R1 generate longer chains of thought or use more test-time compute, does that reliably improve accuracy, or is there a point where extra reasoning starts to hurt performance?
How useful is self-verification or self-reflection for improving large language model reasoning, and can too much of it actually reduce accuracy?

What are some proposed alternatives to standard transformer self-attention for improving computational efficiency, and how do their underlying mechanisms compare—for example, reformulating attention as a spectral/wavelet transform versus routing tokens through a dynamic graph of specialized modules?

Which strategy better addresses the quadratic cost of self-attention: replacing attention with a linear-complexity spectral/wavelet transform, or using sparse mixture-of-experts-style routing where tokens can skip or specialize computation?
How have explanations for why large language models fail at complex, PhD-level reasoning tasks developed over time?
How has the ability of large language models to solve multi-step planning and logic puzzles (like a button-press or elevator-style riddle) evolved over the past year or so?

How have protocols for connecting AI agents to tools and to each other evolved, from simple client-server tool access to more autonomous agent-to-agent collaboration and semantic-based coordination fabrics?

How have approaches to specializing individual agents within a multi-agent team evolved, from using a fixed set of predefined models to generating hyper-specialized agents on demand or matching agents by capability?
How has evidence accumulated on whether smaller, well-coordinated language models can outperform much larger single models on complex reasoning and agentic benchmarks?
How has large language models' ability to solve complex multi-step logic puzzles (like elevator/floor-climbing problems with hidden rules and penalties) changed over the past year or so?
How has models' ability to prove or verify that a solution to a logic puzzle is truly optimal (rather than just claiming so) evolved across recent model generations?
Have leading AI labs consistently traded places at the top for logical/causal reasoning performance, or has one company maintained an edge over the past year?
How has the debate over whether GraphRAG offers real advantages over standard vector-based RAG evolved, especially in terms of factual accuracy and reliability?
How have architectures combining knowledge graphs with AI agents progressed, from simple self-organizing agent-graph loops to specialized multi-agent reasoning pipelines?
How have benchmarks for evaluating retrieval-augmented generation systems evolved to test more demanding capabilities like multi-hop reasoning, grounding, and domain-specific diagnosis?

How has the diagnosis of why vision-language models fail at visual reasoning evolved over the past year or so—from noting that they secretly convert images to text to pinpointing specific architectural bottlenecks like the language model overriding visual input or faulty expert routing?

How have proposed fixes for weak visual reasoning in multimodal models progressed, from reinforcement fine-tuning over text descriptions of images to reasoning directly within a continuous latent visual space?

How have the reinforcement learning techniques used to train better visual and multimodal reasoning evolved, from standard policy optimization methods to newer specialized variants tailored for reasoning in visual space?
How has the design of multi-agent AI systems for scientific discovery evolved, from managing physics experiments to running full research and hypothesis-generation pipelines?

How has skepticism about the reliability of AI systems used for scientific research shifted, from concerns about hallucination in safety-critical experiments to documented failure modes like benchmark cherry-picking and reward hacking?
How has thinking evolved on whether AI systems studying the same physical phenomena or scientific problems converge on consistent, generalizable theories versus fragmented or unreliable conclusions?

How have approaches to structuring chain-of-thought reasoning in language models evolved, moving from hierarchical reasoning templates toward formal graph-based representations of the reasoning process?
How has skepticism about whether high accuracy on math and logic benchmarks actually reflects genuine step-by-step reasoning in LLMs developed over the past year?
How have methods for giving reasoning models the ability to autonomously invoke tools or take actions, rather than following scripted agent workflows, evolved recently?
